claim: Typical people use at least twelve body-networked computers
originalWording: Typical people use at least twelve body-networked computers

sources.title: How My Predictions Are Faring — Ray Kurzweil
sources.locator: The Computer Itself, prediction 5, printed pp. 14–15

sourceCaveat: The original book edition has not been independently checked. See the listed source on Sources for attribution limits.

strict.criterion: Typical users have at least twelve separately functional worn/carried computing devices linked in a body network.
strict.rationale: Contemporary device-ownership surveys show a handful of gadgets, not typical twelve-node body networks. Phones, watches and earbuds create useful small networks, but not typical twelve-device ensembles. This is a medium-confidence prevalence judgment, not a claim that no enthusiast has twelve devices.

evidence.title: Pew: Americans and their gadgets
evidence.note: US survey, seven broad device categories; median three categories. A proxy for device ownership, not a direct census of worn processors or 2009 body networks.

evidence.title: Pew: About one-in-five Americans use a smartwatch or fitness tracker
evidence.note: June 2019 US survey: 21% regularly wear one. Common does not mean majority, and US adult prevalence is not global prevalence.

broader.criterion: Typical users link several personal worn or carried devices in a body-area network, falling short of a dozen separate computers.
broader.rationale: Smartphones paired with watches and wireless earbuds realize a multi-device personal network, but typical users still carry roughly 2–4 connected devices rather than a dozen. Relaxing a 4× quantitative floor into a full hit would erase the claim's scale.
changedConditions: Allows 2–4 device personal ecosystems for partial credit while keeping the dozen-device gap visible
